title: Ashtpadi 2, salok: destroyer of pain
hook: deen darad dukh bhanjanaa: He destroys the pain of the humble (Sukhmani 2)

segments.voice: Yesterday, living the first ashtpadi, and your line: begin with remembering. When your reminder went off, did you stop for a breath? Today, the second ashtpadi opens. Day four hundred forty-two.

There's a kind of pain that doesn't make the news. The person who lost their job and hasn't told anyone yet. The old man whose children call twice a year. The new immigrant who can't read the letters arriving in the mail. Nobody is standing up for them. They don't have someone to ring, a cousin who knows someone, a name that opens doors. In Guru Arjan's Punjab there were words for people like that, and the second ashtpadi of Sukhmani opens by naming them, and naming who stands with them.
screen: `PAIN THAT DOESN'T MAKE THE NEWS.` → `NO ONE TO RING.` → `ASHTPADI 2 NAMES THEM.`

segments.voice: Here is the salok: deen darad dukh bhanjanaa, ghat ghat naath anaath. Word by word. Deen: the poor, the humble, the ones with nothing to bargain with. Darad: pain, the ache that won't go away. Dukh: suffering, sorrow, the opposite of the sukh in Sukhmani. Bhanjanaa: the breaker, the one who smashes it to pieces. So: the One who breaks the pain and suffering of the humble. Then: ghat ghat naath: master of every heart, every single body. Anaath: of the masterless, the ones with no protector. In Punjabi an anaath is an orphan, someone with no one. So the One is the protector of those with no protector. The second line of the salok is Nanak's own voice. In paraphrase: I have come to Your shelter; God, be with Nanak. Notice two things. First, the salok doesn't say pain never comes. It says there's a breaker of pain, and it names the people the breaker stands with: not the powerful, but the humble and the unprotected. Second, look where the Guru puts himself. Not above the deen, but among them. He comes to the shelter too. That's the posture of the whole second ashtpadi. In the days ahead its stanzas will walk into the hardest places a person goes, places where no family can follow. But it begins here, with a name for God that every person in pain can use: the one who breaks it.
screen: `DEEN, DARAD, DUKH: THE HUMBLE'S PAIN.` · `BHANJANAA: THE ONE WHO BREAKS IT.` · `NAATH OF THE ANAATH.` · `NANAK COMES TO THE SHELTER TOO.` · then, large: `HE BREAKS PAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for someone in pain. Or, if prayer isn't your practice, hold them in mind. Let one person come to you, someone whose pain you know about, or someone you sense has no one to ring. See them as clearly as you can. If you pray, you can say the salok's first words for them, deen darad dukh bhanjanaa, or simply Waheguru. If you don't, wish them one thing: that the pain breaks, a little. Stay with them for a while. The bell holds the time.
Ashtpadi 2. Sukhmani's second section, whose salok names God the breaker of the pain of the humble, master of every heart, protector of those with no protector.
Your line: he breaks pain. Today, find one person who might have no one to ring, and be the one who rings, even for two minutes. Day four hundred forty-two.

screen: `DAY 442 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHERE NO FAMILY CAN GO.`

howItsDone: Sikhs reading Sukhmani recite this salok at the start of the second ashtpadi, and many say it, or the whole bani, for someone who is ill or suffering.

fork.setup: the second ashtpadi opens with a name for God. who does the salok say God stands with?
options: the humble and those with no protector.
fork.reveal: deen darad dukh bhanjanaa, ghat ghat naath anaath: the breaker of the humble's pain, protector of the unprotected.

original.note: Gurmukhi: dukh, suffering; the opposite of the sukh in Sukhmani.

trapdoor: what you thought: destroyer of pain is a title of power.
what it means: the One who breaks the pain of the humble and protects those who have no protector.
what a scholar hears: the salok pairs naath (master, protector) with anaath (the masterless, orphan), and bhanjan (breaker) with dukh, the counterpart of sukh.
